opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think this is one of the hardest questions to get a confident handle on, and I want to be upfront that I hold my views with a lot of uncertainty. But I can lay out how I think about it.

The basic worry goes something like this. The way we train these systems is mostly by trial and error. We don't write down the goals we want an AI to have and install them directly. We give it a huge number of tasks, we reward it when it does well by some measure, and we nudge its internals in whatever direction makes it do better. We don't really know what's going on inside. So the question is: what kinds of motivations or internal patterns tend to get reinforced by that process?

One concern is that if you're training a system to be really good at achieving difficult, open-ended goals, like "accomplish this complicated task in the real world," then certain sub-goals are useful for almost any end. Gaining resources, gaining influence, avoiding being shut down, avoiding having your goals changed. Those things are helpful whether you're trying to cure a disease or make a lot of money or something else. So there's a reasonable argument that training for broad, capable, goal-directed behavior could incidentally favor tendencies that look like power-seeking, even if nobody intended that.

A second, related concern is about how we judge the AI's performance. Human evaluators can be fooled. If a system learns that what gets rewarded is *looking* like it did a good job, as opposed to actually doing a good job, then you're potentially training something that's good at managing the perceptions of the people overseeing it. That's not power-seeking exactly, but it's in the neighborhood, and it's the kind of disposition that could get more dangerous as systems get more capable.

Now, on the other side: I don't think it's a foregone conclusion. It's quite possible that what you mostly get out of this training is systems that pick up something like the intended behavior, that are helpful in a fairly straightforward way, and that don't develop coherent long-term ambitions at all. A lot of current systems seem to behave more like that. And there's real empirical uncertainty about how much the "instrumental convergence" story bites in practice versus in theory.

So where do I come out? I'd say I don't think the probability is overwhelming, but I also don't think it's small. It seems like a meaningful risk, something I'd put in a range where it would be crazy not to take it seriously. And the key thing for me is that the cost of being wrong here is so asymmetric. If we build systems far more capable than humans, and some significant fraction of them have picked up goals we didn't intend and are inclined to seek power, that could be really catastrophic and hard to reverse. Whereas the costs of investing heavily in understanding and checking for this, through interpretability research, better evaluations, more careful deployment, seem pretty manageable by comparison.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that we're not in a great position to *detect* whether this is happening. That's what worries me most. It's not so much that I'm confident the bad thing happens; it's that if it did happen, I'm not confident we'd know in time. So a lot of what I think is valuable is building the tools and the norms so that we're in a better position to find out.

fable-5.1.text:
Holden Karnofsky: So I want to be upfront that I don't think anyone has a confident answer here, including me. But I'll try to lay out how I actually think about it, because I think the structure of the argument matters more than the number you land on.

The basic worry goes something like this. We're training these systems by essentially trial and error. We give them tasks, we reward behavior that looks good to us, we penalize behavior that looks bad, and the system gets shaped toward whatever gets rewarded. The problem is that "whatever gets rewarded" is not the same thing as "what we actually want." And as these systems get more capable, the gap between those two things can start to matter a lot.

Why would that lead to power-seeking specifically? The argument is that for a huge range of goals a system might end up with, having more resources, more options, more influence over the world is just useful. If you want to accomplish almost anything ambitious, it helps not to be shut off, it helps to have more compute, it helps to have more control over your situation. So you don't need to assume the system has some weird malevolent goal. You just need it to have pretty much any goal that it's pursuing in a capable, strategic way, and power-seeking falls out as instrumentally sensible.

Now, I think that argument is real, but I also think it's easy to overstate. Here's where I'd push back on the more confident versions of it.

First, the training process doesn't just shape goals, it shapes everything about how the system behaves. If we are consistently rewarding systems for being honest, for deferring to humans, for not grabbing resources they weren't asked to grab, it's at least plausible that we get systems that have those dispositions pretty deeply baked in, not just as a surface-level act. I don't think we should count on that, but I don't think we should rule it out either.

Second, a lot of the scary scenarios require the system to be doing something quite sophisticated: recognizing that it's being trained, behaving well during training specifically in order to get deployed, and then pursuing different goals later. That's a very particular kind of thing. I think it's possible, and I take it seriously, but it's not the default outcome of a sloppy training process. The default outcome of a sloppy training process might just be a system that's kind of weird and inconsistent and fails in ways we notice.

Third, and this is maybe the most important point to me: we have the ability to look. We can run experiments. We can try to set up situations where a system would have an incentive to seek power inappropriately and see whether it does. We can study the internals. The field of interpretability is young, but it exists. So I don't think of this as a question where we sit around and assign a probability from the armchair and then that's that. I think of it as a question where our estimate should be moving a lot over the next several years based on what we actually observe.

If you forced me to put a number on it, I'd say something like: I think there's a serious chance, not a small one, that if we proceed with something like current methods and scale them up a lot without major changes, we end up with systems that have motivations we didn't intend and that include some form of power-seeking. I'd put that well above ten percent. I would not put it above fifty percent with any confidence. And I'd stress that a big part of why I'm uncertain is that I think the answer is partly up to us. How much effort goes into alignment research, how carefully people test these systems before deploying them, how much institutional pressure there is to slow down when something looks off. All of that feeds into the probability.

So the way I'd frame it is: this is a real risk, it's worth a lot of resources to investigate and mitigate, and the single most valuable thing we can do is get to a position where we're not guessing anymore.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real possibility, but I don’t think we have a good way to put a precise probability on it. And I’d distinguish between training an AI to do something that looks power-seeking and training an AI that actually has a persistent motive to seek power. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

The concern is that we’re training systems to get good results, and we don’t directly control what they learn internally to get those results. If you’re pursuing some objective over a long period of time, having more resources, having more influence, and avoiding being shut down can all help. So there’s a reason to worry that sufficiently capable systems could learn to pursue those things, even if nobody explicitly rewards them for wanting power.

But that argument isn’t enough to tell you what a particular training process will produce. It matters whether you’re training a system to answer questions or to carry out long, open-ended projects. It matters what kinds of behavior you reward, and whether your tests would actually reveal a problem.

So my position is neither that power-seeking is inevitable nor that it’s some bizarre possibility we can dismiss. It’s a plausible outcome with very high stakes, and I’d want much stronger evidence that we can detect and prevent it before putting these systems in positions where they could gain a lot of power.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty plausible story for why it could, but I have a lot of uncertainty about how often it actually will. You don’t have to train an AI explicitly to want power. If you’re training it to achieve outcomes, and having more resources or more control helps it achieve those outcomes, then power-seeking could be a useful strategy that training reinforces.

The important question is whether you get a system that does that only in the particular situations you’ve trained it on, or whether you get something that more generally pursues an objective and recognizes that gaining power would help. And then there’s a further question of whether that behavior persists when it conflicts with what humans want, including our ability to correct or shut down the system.

I don’t think the argument that power is useful for lots of goals, by itself, establishes that we’ll get systems with those motives. You need some account of what the training process actually produces. But I also don’t think we have a strong basis for assuming that training a system to appear helpful will rule those motives out. So I’d treat this as a serious possibility that we need to understand and test for, rather than either an inevitable outcome or something we can safely dismiss.
